paras: The Cowtown attack on the Washington poundmen was an assault by a crowd of residents of the 'Cowtown' neighborhood of Washington, D.C., on the city poundmaster and his men on the morning of August 19, 1882, in which a Black poundman, Albert Fortune, was struck on the head with a stone. During the fray a resident, John Keefe, called for a gun to 'kill the niggers', and four residents were fined or forfeited collateral in Police Court.

Poundmaster Einstein, his 'colored assistants' and Policeman Farquhar went to Cowtown, just above Boundary street near Sherman avenue, to impound loose animals, and surrounded fifteen dogs and a flock of geese in a nearby creek. The Evening Star described it as 'another warm reception' for the poundmen, implying earlier resistance elsewhere.

At about 5 o'clock by the Star's first report, or 6 o'clock by Einstein's later testimony, residents drove off the dogs before they could be loaded into the wagon. When the poundmen turned to the geese, women came out armed with paving stones, sticks and table-knives, the men joined them, and one woman cut the tail nearly off Einstein's coat. According to Einstein, a young man named Patrick Murphy threw a large stone that struck Fortune on the head and then retreated into a cornfield.

When Einstein, the policeman and the poundmen followed Murphy, Keefe came out, ordered them out of the field and called for a gun so that he could 'kill the niggers'; the Evening Critic gave his words as a threat to 'chase the —— niggers off the hill.' The poundmen withdrew, taking Murphy prisoner, and Keefe and David Nelligan were also arrested.

Nelligan forfeited collateral the same day, and the cases of Murphy and Keefe were continued so the defense could gather witnesses. On August 22 Judge Bundy fined Keefe $2 or 7 days for profanity, and fined his daughter Maggie Long $5 or 15 days for obstructing the poundmaster after the pound party testified that she led the crowd with a stone. Murphy was fined $5 or 15 days for assaulting Fortune and noted an appeal, and Maggie Long's husband, Patrick H. Long, forfeited collateral the next day. No report of the outcome of Murphy's appeal was found.

Only two Washington dailies were found to carry the story, the Evening Star on August 19, 22 and 23 and the Evening Critic on August 23. The Star treated the first clash as comedy under the headline 'The Pound War,' writing of the 'natives' of a 'usually quiet "burg"' and of poundmen 'retreating in good order.' Its trial report identified Fortune as one of Einstein's 'colored assistants' and printed Keefe's slur in full, though it also once called the victim 'Albert Dodson.' The Critic, headlining its item 'Pounding the Poundmen,' called the episode a 'mob attack' and identified Murphy as 'a young white man.'

Defense witnesses testified that Murphy had been assaulted by one of the Black poundmen, and Murphy said he owned no geese, his dog was tagged and he was only a spectator; the court nonetheless found him guilty of assault.

reader.title: Cowtown attack on the Washington poundmen
bases: A crowd of residents attacked the poundmaster's party with stones, sticks and knives, and a Black poundman, Albert Fortune, was struck on the head with a stone; no one was killed (A1, A2, A3).

The Evening Star's same-day report and trial report and the Evening Critic's separate Police Court report agree on the crowd attack, the stone striking Fortune, Keefe's threat and the fines (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: Poundmaster, policeman and Black poundmen (prosecution testimony)
accounts.gist: A large crowd drove off the dogs and geese; Murphy threw a stone that struck Fortune; Keefe called for a gun to 'kill the niggers'; Maggie Long led the crowd with a stone.

accounts.label: Defense witnesses and Murphy
accounts.gist: Witnesses said Murphy was assaulted by one of the colored poundmen; Murphy said he had no geese, his dog wore a tag, and he was only a spectator.

accounts.label: Evening Star local report
accounts.gist: A humorous same-day account of the 'natives' and armed women routing the poundmen, with Murphy striking a poundman with a stone.

framing.detail: The Evening Star headlined it 'The Pound War' and 'A Sharp Engagement in "Cowtown"', describing the 'usually quiet "burg"' and the poundmen 'retreating in good order' in mock-military terms, while printing Keefe's slur in its trial report.
The Evening Critic, under 'Pounding the Poundmen', called it a 'mob attack' and identified Murphy as 'a young white man'.

conflicts.note: The Star uses both names in the same report; the Critic uses Fortune, so 'Dodson' is likely an error.
